newsitem.title: UK: Zeneca sees no need for strategic takeovers.
newsitem.headline: Zeneca sees no need for strategic takeovers.

text.p: British drugs and chemicals company Zeneca Group Plc said on Wednesday it saw no need for strategic acquisitions, and had yet to come across any takeover opportunities which offered both "value and quality." In his last interview before the group enters its closed reporting period ahead of full year results on March 11, chief executive David Barnes told Reuters, "I am not against acquisitions per se but they have to offer value and quality, and most of the opportunites that have come up have failed on one or both criteria."

Barnes also underlined his confidence in the group's ability to meet his "inspirational target" of effectively doubling profit in the next five years, with all three businesses contributing to the improvement.

Barnes said Zeneca's focus is the roll-out of a raft of new products, including asthma drug Accolate, schizophrenia drug Seroquel and its new agro-chemical fungicide Amistar, which he described as "the biggest single product we've got in the Zeneca portfolio."

"I do not wish to divert resources from that major task into either some terrible slash-and-burn type operation or some dilutive-type operation," he said. "If I saw a good quality opportunity I hope we would have the conviction and determination to (take it), but what I haven't seen so far is that good quality opportunity."

Zeneca is thought to have looked at a wide variety of companies in recent years, including Wellcome Plc, Fisons Plc and the pharmaceutical arm of Boots Plc. It is also believed to have talked separately to both Pharmacia of Sweden and Upjohn of the U.S. before the two companies merged in 1995.

Barnes told Reuters the company would concentrate on building up its product and technology platform through alliances and licensing deals, including with the biotech sector. Zeneca already has links with Celltech Group Plc, British Biotech Plc and Sugen Inc, and Barnes said further "small" deals will be announced this year.

"What we are trying to do is get access to technology platforms or programmes and I do not see us buying 100 percent of a biotech comapny. I'd rather have eight different types of alliances with eight different biotechs than own any one of them 100 percent," he added.

Barnes said he believed a takeover bid for Zeneca itself was "most unlikely," but added that in the end "remaining independent is a matter for Zeneca shareholders to determine, not me." Speculation over the past year has linked Zeneca as a takeover or merger candidate with a dizzying number of partners, including Switzerland's Roche Holdings AG, Germany's Bayer AG and France's Sanofi.

The chief executive said any offer would have to be compared with Zeneca's own targets for increasing shareholder value "and if we achieve or get close to the aspirational target I have set that means doubling the profit every five years."

Barnes's announcement last year that he wanted to increase Zeneca's earnings per share by an average of 15 percent over the next five years was initially met with some cynicism by analysts, who saw it as a way of frightening off would-be predators. However, it has been increasingly accepted as a realistic goal.

Barnes said the 15 percent target was "not a forecast. My task is to put a bit of inspirational stretch in, like training an athlete." Barnes said Zeneca's first-half results and nine-months trading statement showed "we were in line for achieving that in 1996, and I don't think anything has changed dramatically since we made the nine month statement. I think it's a credible target."
